job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Drafting review: S. 2817 (manager's amendment, Oct. 6, 2026)**

This review is based only on the text you pasted. I haven't checked the official bill text, CRS analysis, or the statutes it references (such as 1 U.S.C. § 1 and 28 U.S.C. § 2462), so please verify those before publication.

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The 10^26 threshold applies only to "a single training run," so a developer could split one program into several runs or stages to stay under it. "Trained using" is also unclear about whether continued pretraining, fine-tuning, or distillation counts.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The bill doesn't specify how compute is measured (precision, sparsity, whether inference counts) and gives no agency authority to define it. Any enforcement action would turn on this disputed measurement.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The compute threshold is fixed in statute with no mechanism to update it. Algorithmic efficiency gains could bring comparably capable systems below 10^26.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** "The Secretary" is never identified. The bill mentions the Secretary of State (Sec. 6) and the Department of Commerce (Sec. 4), but this section doesn't say who makes determinations.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** The determination process has no procedure, notice requirement, evaluation standard, or timeline, and it doesn't say whether determinations apply prospectively or retroactively. Developers can't know in advance whether they're covered, and the determinations are open to APA challenge.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** "Capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks" has no measurable benchmark. Phrases like "most cognitive tasks" are vague enough to support either side in litigation.

7. **Sec. 2(1):** Clause (A) uses "artificial intelligence model" and clause (B) uses "artificial intelligence system," and neither term is defined. A model with scaffolding or tools might be read as covered under one clause and not the other.

8. **Sec. 2(2):** "U.S. person" covers only citizens and state-chartered corporations. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, and other non-corporate entities, as well as foreign-incorporated affiliates of U.S. firms. "State" is also undefined, so it's unclear whether D.C. and the territories are included.

9. **Sec. 2(3):** "Advanced AI chips," "data center," and "containing" are undefined. Operators could spread chips across multiple sites or rent cloud capacity so that no single facility exceeds 50,000 chips, and the bill has no aggregation rule.

10. **Sec. 2(3) and Sec. 4:** The registry covers only "covered facilities," which are defined by chip count, while covered systems are defined by training compute. A developer could train a covered system at a site below the chip threshold and fall outside the registry entirely.

11. **Sec. 3(a):** "Train," "develop," and "deploy" are undefined. It's unclear whether releasing weights, offering API access, or publishing an open-weight model counts as deployment, and "any person in the United States" could reach ordinary users who run a covered model. Those ambiguities also create vagueness and First Amendment challenge risk for the criminal provision.

12. **Sec. 3(a):** The prohibition reaches U.S. persons abroad but not foreign developers operating outside the U.S. Those developers are covered only if the Sec. 6 agreement materializes, which the bill doesn't guarantee.

13. **Sec. 3(b):** The grandfather clause turns on when training "began" (undefined), not when it ends or when deployment starts. It also exempts all of subsection (a), so further development and deployment of grandfathered systems are unrestricted, and no registration or reporting is required. Combined with the 180-day delay in Sec. 8, this creates an incentive to start large training runs before the effective date.

14. **Sec. 3(c):** "Safety evaluation" is undefined, and "activities conducted for the purpose of" is subjective and hard to prove or disprove. The exemption has no limits on scale, duration, qualifications, or reporting, and no requirement to stop if an evaluation finds danger. It also doesn't say whether training a model in order to evaluate it is exempt.

15. **Sec. 4(a):** "Operator" is undefined, and the bill sets no registration deadline.

16. **Sec. 4(b):** Reports must describe "computing workloads" but don't require identifying whether any workload is a covered AI system. The bill also doesn't specify report content, give any verification or audit authority, set a filing deadline, or protect trade secrets. There's no stated penalty for a false certification.

17. **Secs. 4 and 5(a):** No penalty applies to failing to register or report, because Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. The registry therefore has no direct enforcement mechanism.

18. **Sec. 5(a):** The bill names no enforcing agency and no procedure (administrative or judicial). It also omits injunctive authority, forfeiture of compute, weights, or facilities, and any limitations period. The default five-year limit under 28 U.S.C. § 2462 may apply, which should be verified.

19. **Sec. 5(a):** "For each day on which the violation occurs" doesn't say how days are counted for continuing violations, such as a training run that lasts months, or whether each system or facility is a separate violation. The penalty amount also has no inflation adjustment.

20. **Secs. 5(a) and 8:** Penalties apply to violations "occurring on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 3 doesn't take effect until 180 days after enactment. The two provisions conflict on timing, and the enactment reference is confusing because no Sec. 3 violation can occur before the effective date.

21. **Sec. 5(b):** "Willfully" is undefined: it's unclear whether it requires knowledge of the law or only knowing conduct. The bill also has no provisions on corporate officer liability, aiding and abetting, conspiracy, or liability for cloud or chip providers who knowingly enable violations.

22. **Sec. 6:** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no obligation to succeed, no reporting requirement, and no consequence for failure. "Equivalent" is undefined, so the provision gives no enforcement tool.

23. **Sec. 7(a) and Sec. 7(b):** These conflict. Sec. 7(a) keeps the prohibition in place until Congress passes a joint resolution, but Sec. 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years whether or not that resolution passes.

24. **Sec. 7(a):** The bill sets no deadline for the NASEM report and doesn't require one to be produced. "Can be developed safely" is undefined, and there's no expedited procedure for the joint resolution, so the lifting mechanism may be practically unusable.

25. **Sec. 7(b):** The sunset runs from enactment, but Sec. 8 delays effectiveness by 180 days, so the operative period is about 9.5 years. The bill has no savings clause for pre-sunset violations, pending investigations, or accrued penalties, and no rule for grandfathered systems after the sunset.

26. **Whole bill:** The bill has no rulemaking authority (for compute measurement, registry forms, or determinations), no judicial review provision, no severability clause (a successful challenge to one provision, such as Sec. 2(1)(B), could jeopardize the whole Act), no savings or preemption clause, no appropriation, and no whistleblower protections.

**Highest-priority items for the piece:** 13 (grandfathering plus the 180-day window), 10 (registry gap), 23 (sunset conflict), 1 and 9 (threshold splitting), 4 through 6 (discretionary determinations), 17 (no penalty for registry violations), and 20 (timing conflict).

**Balance note:** This list concentrates on enforceability and gaps, which is the question you asked. Several items, especially 11, 14, and 5, also raise overbreadth concerns that could matter to research and open-source communities. If the piece is going to be read as balanced, it should give those concerns equal weight. Before publication, I'd also recommend having the drafting points checked by someone with Senate Legislative Counsel or CRS experience.
